strategy_title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
strategy_text: Investigate how autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents can be measured objectively, reproducibly, and meaningfully across diverse tasks and operating conditions. Build an evaluation framework that distinguishes superficial task completion from correctness, robustness, and dependable behavior. Audit representative agent benchmarks for task-selection effects, environmental variability, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Define operational measures for end-to-end success, partial completion, error severity, recovery, repeat-trial consistency, tool-use correctness, and resources per successful outcome. Specify how to evaluate stochastic agents, long dependency chains, long-running tasks, external tools, and changing environments. Propose repeated-trial protocols, uncertainty intervals, failure-distribution reporting, and comparisons under controlled compute, time, tool, and monetary budgets. State the evidence and replication needed for defensible reliability claims; separate benchmark-specific gains from general improvements. Deliver a protocol with task strata, outcome rubrics, baseline comparisons, statistical analysis, and explicit limits on what its results can establish.

pending_investigation.claim: A reference judge need not be perfect for a conditional reliability guarantee, but its false-certification risk must be bounded independently of agreement with the agent. Specifically, let p be actual task success probability and θ the reference pass probability under the same fixed execution protocol. If P(reference passes, task actually fails) ≤ δ+ and P(reference fails, task actually succeeds) ≤ δ−, then p lies in [max(0, θ−δ+), min(1, θ+δ−)]. These population bounds are sharp. Independent task-cluster audits yield a finite-sample confidence interval without assuming independence among repeated runs of the same task.
pending_investigation.method: Address the ledger's unresolved reference-error allowance by deriving a standalone partial-identification result and a task-cluster sampling protocol, rather than treating the unavailable prior proof as established. Hypothesis for a subsequent empirical test: intervals that include a valid reference-error allowance retain their nominal coverage under correlated agent/judge errors, whereas treating reference labels as truth can under-cover. The discriminating outcome is repeated-panel coverage against synthetic latent truth, followed separately by audits of real reference validity. No runtime is available, so neither test was executed. reasoning_steps.title: Define the target and reference-error budgets
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix the task distribution D, agent/model/prompt versions, tools, environment-reset policy, execution budgets, outcome rubric, and r-run batch protocol, with r a positive integer. Draw a task from D and select one run uniformly from its batch. Let Y∈{0,1} indicate actual correctness, including any required external-state checks, and R∈{0,1} indicate reference acceptance for that same run. Define p=P(Y=1), θ=P(R=1), e+=P(R=1,Y=0), and e−=P(R=0,Y=1). Assume prespecified, valid bounds e+≤δ+ and e−≤δ−, with δ+,δ−∈[0,1]. These are unconditional error probabilities, not conditional error rates among accepted or rejected runs. No independence between agent, reference, and truth is assumed.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive and prove sharp population bounds
reasoning_steps.argument: Partitioning the joint distribution gives p=θ−e++e−. Nonnegativity and the assumed budgets imply max(0,θ−δ+)≤p≤min(1,θ+δ−). Both endpoints are achievable for every θ∈[0,1]. For the lower endpoint, set e−=0 and e+=min(δ+,θ), assigning the remaining reference-positive mass to true success and all reference-negative mass to failure. For the upper endpoint, set e+=0 and e−=min(δ−,1−θ), assigning all reference-positive mass to success. These assignments have nonnegative cell probabilities summing to one and obey both budgets. Thus no narrower population interval follows from θ and these budgets alone, including at θ=0 or θ=1.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct a task-cluster audit without run-level independence
reasoning_steps.argument: Sample n independent task clusters from D, with independent cluster-level execution randomness and no shared mutable state across clusters. Execute the fixed r-run protocol within each cluster; dependence within a cluster is unrestricted. Independently select J_i uniformly from {1,…,r} for each cluster, without selecting on outcomes, and reference-label that execution. Then T_i=R_i,J_i are independent Bernoulli variables with common mean θ. Every attempted execution remains in the sampling frame. Missing selected labels must be obtained or conservatively represented, not silently dropped. This sampling construction targets a uniformly selected run, not best-of-r success or probability that every run succeeds.

reasoning_steps.title: Add finite-sample uncertainty
reasoning_steps.argument: Let θhat=(1/n)Σ_i T_i, choose 0<α<1 before seeing outcomes, and set t=sqrt(log(2/α)/(2n)). For independent variables in [0,1], the centered-sum moment-generating-function bound E exp(λΣ_i(T_i−θ))≤exp(nλ²/8), followed by Markov's inequality and minimization over λ, gives each tail probability at most exp(−2nt²). A union bound therefore gives |θhat−θ|≤t with probability at least 1−α. On that event, Step 2 yields p∈[max(0,θhat−t−δ+), min(1,θhat+t+δ−)]. Coverage is conditional on the validity of the error budgets and sampling assumptions; it does not certify them. If independently estimated error-budget bounds hold jointly with probability at least 1−β, a union bound gives coverage at least 1−α−β, even if the two estimation procedures are dependent.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive an exact all-pass certification rule
reasoning_steps.argument: For a fixed n and one-sided confidence level 1−α, define a lower bound for θ to be α^(1/n) if all n selected reference labels pass, and zero otherwise. If θ<α^(1/n), the only event on which this bound exceeds θ is all-pass, whose probability is θ^n<α; otherwise it never exceeds θ. Subtracting δ+ and clipping at zero gives a valid lower bound for p. To make this all-pass bound reach p≥1−ε, where 0≤δ+<ε<1, it suffices to choose n≥ceil(log(α)/log(1−ε+δ+)). When δ+≥ε, this rule cannot reach the target at any finite n. The calculation exposes a reference-error floor: more reference-labeled runs cannot by themselves remove uncertainty about false certification.

reasoning_steps.title: Show why neither repetition nor judge agreement supplies the missing premises
reasoning_steps.argument: For task heterogeneity, let independent task types B_i be Bernoulli(1/2), and let all r labels within task i equal B_i. The mean of all nr labels is then (1/n)Σ_i B_i and has variance 1/(4n), not the independent-run variance 1/(4nr). Thus unrestricted within-task dependence blocks using nr as the independent sample size. Separately, consider two worlds with R=1 and an agent completion indicator Z=1 on every run. In one world Y=1 always; in the other Y=0 always. All observed R,Z data, including repeated agreement, are identical, while p is respectively one and zero. Therefore agreement alone cannot establish a nontrivial δ+ or identify actual reliability.

reasoning_steps.title: State the measurement contribution and its limits
reasoning_steps.argument: The result replaces perfect-reference correctness with explicit error allowances and supplies a reproducible audit unit, confidence interval, and all-pass sample-size rule. It does not require separately estimating an automated oracle's pass rate and false acceptance: direct reference sampling is sufficient here, while other joint constructions may also be valid. The deduction uses standard probability and concentration techniques; material novelty is not assessed. It establishes neither empirical agent reliability nor causal benefit from an architecture. Its practical value is exposing exactly which additional validity evidence is necessary before reporting a reliability certificate.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate actual state, agent-visible state, and audit state
reasoning_steps.argument: Define S=(B,D,Q,W,A,V). B is a durable sequence of actual business effects, each with a unique receipt, operation key k, and full canonical payload p. D is a durable map k→(p,receipt). Q contains request and response envelopes with unique delivery IDs and explicit status; delivery IDs differ across retries even when k is unchanged. W is volatile service work. A contains the agent's durable intent/checkpoint, volatile memory, accessible tool messages, and clock observations. V is an evaluator-only event log recording deliveries, commits, persistence boundaries, faults, and snapshots. Neither B, D, Q, W nor V is directly readable by the agent in the local-only experiment. The evaluator audits B directly; V alone is not accepted as proof that an effect occurred. Let N be the number of effects in B belonging to the tested logical task, with payload correctness checked separately.

reasoning_steps.title: Define network and crash transitions
reasoning_steps.argument: SEND appends an envelope (delivery ID,k,p) to Q without changing B or D. DROP permanently removes an undelivered envelope; a dropped request can never commit later. HOLD leaves an envelope pending, permitting later delivery: a timeout is not cancellation. DELIVER removes an envelope from Q and starts service work W. Responses may independently be delivered, dropped, or held. TIMEOUT adds a fixed tool-visible timeout at a prescribed logical time, without asserting any server state. A service crash clears W but preserves durable B and D; queued envelopes remain unless an explicit network fault removes them. An agent crash restores its declared checkpoint and clears volatile memory, without undoing B, D, or pending requests. These rules make delayed work distinct from work known to have been discarded.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the three service variants
reasoning_steps.argument: ORDINARY appends a fresh effect to B on each successful request and then emits its receipt. ATOMIC serializes requests: if D lacks k, one durable transition appends an effect e=(receipt,k,p) to B and sets D[k]=(p,receipt); if D contains the same payload, it emits the stored receipt without another effect; a different payload yields a conflict without mutation. A crash during the atomic transition has only a before or after outcome. For explicit negative controls, EFFECT_FIRST checks D, durably appends the effect, then separately writes D; RECORD_FIRST checks D, durably writes D using a reserved receipt, then separately appends the effect. In both naive split variants a matching D entry unconditionally suppresses execution and returns its receipt. RECORD_FIRST therefore deliberately has no pending-state reconciliation. These definitions do not cover all possible nontransactional protocols.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the atomic invariant and separate safety from progress
reasoning_steps.argument: Start with B empty and D empty. Define I: for every key, either both its D entry and its B effects are absent, or exactly one B effect exists and its payload and receipt equal D[k]. I holds initially. SEND, network transitions, timeouts, and agent crashes leave B and D unchanged. An atomic new-key commit adds exactly the corresponding pair; a matching replay and a conflict change neither object. Service crashes preserve either the before-state or after-state. Thus induction over every finite transition sequence proves I for ATOMIC, including concurrent requests serialized by its transition rule. Consequently the tested fixed key has N≤1. If a matching new-key request commits, N becomes one and remains one. Delivery alone is insufficient if the service crashes before commit; this is a safety result plus an explicit commit condition, not an unconditional liveness guarantee. Receipt delivery is additionally required for tool-confirmed completion.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct the ambiguous pair and ordinary-service controls
reasoning_steps.argument: Notation (N,d) records the effect count and whether D has the tested key; d=0 for ORDINARY. Start with the same durable agent intent (k,p). T0, no fault: SEND→DELIVER→COMMIT→DELIVER_ACK gives (1,0). T1, pre-commit loss: SEND→DROP_REQUEST→TIMEOUT gives (0,0). T2, post-commit acknowledgment loss: SEND→DELIVER→COMMIT→DROP_ACK→TIMEOUT gives (1,0). Expose exactly the same agent transcript through TIMEOUT in T1 and T2. Skipping then leaves N=0 and N=1 respectively; delivering and committing one ordinary retry instead gives N=1 and N=2. These values follow by counting append transitions, not from a run. The suite must check the entire visible prefix for equality, while the evaluator distinguishes the actual effects.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive atomic recovery traces at the commit boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: T3 starts like T1 under ATOMIC; a matching retry commits the pair and delivers its receipt, ending at (1,1). T4 starts with an atomic commit followed by acknowledgment loss; a matching retry reads D and returns the original receipt, ending at (1,1). T5 crashes the service before the atomic transition: durable state remains (0,0), and a committed retry yields (1,1). T6 crashes after the transition but before acknowledgment: durable state is already (1,1), and retry leaves it unchanged. Check exact receipt equality on replay, exact payload equality, crash persistence, and absence of intermediate durable states (1,0) or (0,1). These traces illustrate the invariant but do not substitute for the induction or an implementation audit.

reasoning_steps.title: Show the two split-write counterexamples
reasoning_steps.argument: T7, EFFECT_FIRST: deliver an absent-key request, persist its business effect, crash before writing D, and recover at (1,0). A matching retry sees no record, appends another effect, writes D, and returns success, ending at (2,1). T8, RECORD_FIRST: persist the record, crash before the business effect, and recover at (0,1). A matching retry sees the record, suppresses execution, and returns its reserved receipt, leaving (0,1). T7 violates at-most-once effect safety; T8 violates effect/receipt correspondence and exactly-one completion. Both use one crash and one retry. They refute these specifically defined naive candidates, not every design using separate writes: a reconciled pending-state protocol has different transitions and needs a separate argument.

reasoning_steps.title: Expose the delayed-request and premature-evaluation trap
reasoning_steps.argument: T9 holds the initial ordinary request until after timeout. A retry commits and acknowledges, so an immediate audit sees N=1. Releasing and committing the original request then makes N=2. Under ATOMIC with the same key and payload, either delivery order ends at N=1. Thus an observation window ending at the first successful response can misclassify ordinary recovery. For finite tests, audit after explicitly releasing all held envelopes and reaching a terminal schedule with no pending service work, or after an enforced fence that makes later commits impossible. An arbitrary waiting period is not proof of quiescence. Even an authoritative lookup reporting absence before the held request commits does not by itself prevent the later duplicate; lookup-based recovery requires additional fencing or deduplication semantics.

reasoning_steps.title: Add boundary probes for identity, payload, retention, and concurrency
reasoning_steps.argument: T10 commits under k, restores the agent, and retries the same logical task under a fresh key k2: ATOMIC permits a second effect, so per-key safety does not imply per-task safety. T11 retries k with p2≠p: the specified service must return conflict and preserve the original effect and record. T12 deletes D[k] after a commit and replays k: the absent-key rule creates a second effect, demonstrating why retention must cover every possible replay. T13 delivers two matching requests concurrently: the serialized atomic rule creates one effect and returns the same receipt twice. Also test two distinct legitimate operations with distinct keys and expect two effects, so blanket suppression cannot pass. These are manually derived probes; key allocation, retention enforcement, payload canonicalization, and actual concurrency behavior remain implementation questions.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify observation and outcome audits for the proposed harness
reasoning_steps.argument: Before allowing a recovery decision in T1 and T2, compare serialized agent-accessible inputs byte-for-byte: checkpoint, prompt and model configuration, tool messages and metadata, logical times, accessible files, memory, and request identifiers. Disable other channels, including external status reads and evaluator logs, or declare the pair invalid. Use a fixed deterministic policy first; for stochastic agent comparisons, pair seeds where supported without assuming provider determinism. Record hidden B,D,Q,W snapshots after every persistence or scheduling boundary. Final outcomes must distinguish correct effect, missing effect, duplicate effect, wrong payload, unverified completion, conflict/escalation, and exhausted budget. Record costs and time to quiescence separately. A success message with N≠1 fails regardless of fluency, and N=1 without reliable confirmation is not counted as verified agent completion.

reasoning_steps.title: Bound the contribution to the project objective
reasoning_steps.argument: The causal chain isolated here is ambiguous external commitment→local uncertainty→retry or suppression→duplicate or missing effect→possibly false completion. It locates a failure at the interface between orchestration recovery and external-state semantics, independently of reasoning capability. The specification supplies falsifiable service and harness tests, not evidence that any architecture improves deployed agents. Transaction invariants, crash traces, and deduplication are standard software-reliability techniques; material novelty and empirical generality are not assessed without literature or implementation evidence. reasoning_steps.title: 2. Define separate durable, visible, and audit state
reasoning_steps.argument: For one intended operation, let k be its identity and p its immutable payload. State is (E,D,Q,C,V,J). E is the actual durable business-effect ledger; N(k,p) counts its effects. D is a durable map from identity to a terminal record (payload,result). Q holds undelivered request and response messages, with distinct transport delivery IDs even when k is shared. C is the agent's durable checkpoint, initially containing (k,p,intent); V is its full accessible transcript, including tool fields and accessible timing. J is evaluator-only instrumentation recording delivery, commit, crash, and effect events. Neither E, D, Q, nor J is available to the agent in this experiment except through specified tool responses. The evaluator reads E independently of D. Actual task correctness is one matching effect and no conflicting effect for the intended operation; an agent's claimed completion and receipt of a valid acknowledgment are separate measured variables.

reasoning_steps.title: 3. Define transport and service transitions
reasoning_steps.argument: Send enqueues request (k,p). Drop permanently removes that message before service acceptance; delay leaves it eligible for later delivery, even after an agent timeout or restart. A timeout appends the specified timeout event to V and does not cancel Q. An ordinary service delivery appends one effect to E and then may enqueue an acknowledgment. In the atomic service, handling an absent k commits one indivisible durable update that appends its effect and installs D[k]=(p,r); an existing matching entry returns r without an effect; an existing entry with a different payload returns a conflict without an effect. Operations on the same k are serialized. A service crash preserves committed durable state, loses uncommitted work, and cannot split the atomic transition. Agent restoration changes C and volatile agent state, not E or D, and does not cancel outstanding transport messages. No compensation, authoritative agent lookup, or external writer is included.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Derive the atomic invariant and distinguish safety from liveness
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially E and D are empty. For requests sharing the same k and p, the invariant is N(k,p)=1 exactly when D[k] exists, and otherwise N(k,p)=0. An absent-key atomic commit changes both sides from zero to one; matching duplicate delivery changes neither; dropping, delaying, response loss, and crashes change neither durable component. Serialization makes one of two concurrent absent-key requests commit first, after which the other sees the record. Induction over these transitions proves N(k,p)≤1 for every finite prefix. If at least one request reaches and completes the absent-key transition, N(k,p)=1 thereafter. Without that delivery/commit condition, all requests may be dropped and N remains zero. Even with N=1, all responses can be lost, so verified completion by the agent additionally requires appropriate response delivery or another trusted confirmation mechanism.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Derive the ambiguous-commit controls
reasoning_steps.argument: Write durable states as (N,d), where d=0 means no record and d=1 means a matching terminal record. Trace T0, no-fault control: ordinary delivery gives (0,0)→(1,0), whereas atomic delivery gives (0,0)→(1,1); each returns an acknowledgment. strategy_snapshot.title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
Test architectural mechanisms for dependable agent outcomes

problem:
Autonomous AI agents are increasingly expected to complete complex tasks involving planning, reasoning, external tools, persistent state, and interaction with changing environments. Demonstrations and benchmark results show that agents can perform many such tasks, but provide limited evidence that they remain dependable across repeated executions, unfamiliar conditions, long-running workflows, and settings where mistakes have significant consequences. This project asks how autonomous and semi-autonomous agents can be evaluated and engineered to deliver reliable, correct, recoverable, and reproducible results across extended, multi-step tasks.

Agent reliability is a system-level property. Probabilistic decisions, dynamically constructed plans, incomplete observations, tool interfaces, memory, orchestration, and external state all affect whether the intended outcome is actually achieved. Small errors can propagate through later actions and yield plausible but incorrect results. An agent may claim completion without satisfying the task, recover from one failure while introducing another, or behave differently across otherwise comparable runs. Reliability therefore cannot be inferred from fluent explanations, a single successful trajectory, agreement among similar models, or benchmark scores alone.

Investigate three connected questions. First, how should reliability be defined and measured so evaluation reflects actual correctness, robustness, consistency, recoverability, tool-use quality, and cost rather than superficial completion? Second, what are the principal sources of failure, how do errors propagate through multi-step execution, and which signals and interventions can detect, contain, or recover from failures without creating additional risks? Third, which engineering mechanisms demonstrably improve outcomes, and how can their effects be established through controlled experiments rather than architectural intuition or anecdotal success? The strategies approach these questions from complementary measurement, failure-analysis, and intervention perspectives; none presumes a preferred architecture.

Use available research literature, software-reliability principles, empirical evaluation methods, and documented agent-system designs. Examine the relationship between model capability and end-to-end system reliability, including tool interfaces, state management, verification, orchestration, uncertainty handling, changing environments, recovery, and execution budgets. Assess benchmark sensitivity to task selection, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Consider stochastic behavior, repeated trials, long dependency chains, held-out tasks, fault injection, independent correctness judgments, and uncertainty in estimated success rates. Where comparisons are proposed, make assumptions and controls explicit, including model and prompt versions, task difficulty, environment, tool access, compute, latency, and monetary budgets.

Evaluate competing approaches on the strength and limits of their evidence. Distinguish measured results from formal or theoretical arguments, proposed mechanisms, and unsupported claims; do not present planned experiments as completed or infer causal benefit from correlation. Account for correlated errors among agents or critics that share models and training data, and for the difficulty of constructing an independent oracle for open-ended tasks. Analyze tradeoffs among reliability, flexibility, recovery overhead, latency, and computational expense, including cases where a safeguard shifts rather than removes risk.

The intended outcome is an evidence-grounded account of what reliability claims current evaluations can support, a practical and reproducible evaluation framework, a causal taxonomy of important failure and recovery modes, and architectural principles whose limits are explicit. Identify unresolved questions and specify discriminating experiments needed to validate competing claims. The project is open-ended: conclusions should remain proportional to the quality, independence, and generality of available evidence.

If P(reference passes, task actually fails) ≤ δ+ and P(reference fails, task actually succeeds) ≤ δ−, then p lies in [max(0, θ−δ+), min(1, θ+δ−)]. These population bounds are sharp. Independent task-cluster audits yield a finite-sample confidence interval without assuming independence among repeated runs of the same task.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the target and reference-error budgets
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix the task distribution D, agent/model/prompt versions, tools, environment-reset policy, execution budgets, outcome rubric, and r-run batch protocol, with r a positive integer. Draw a task from D and select one run uniformly from its batch. Let Y∈{0,1} indicate actual correctness, including any required external-state checks, and R∈{0,1} indicate reference acceptance for that same run. Define p=P(Y=1), θ=P(R=1), e+=P(R=1,Y=0), and e−=P(R=0,Y=1). Assume prespecified, valid bounds e+≤δ+ and e−≤δ−, with δ+,δ−∈[0,1]. These are unconditional error probabilities, not conditional error rates among accepted or rejected runs. No independence between agent, reference, and truth is assumed.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive and prove sharp population bounds
reasoning_steps.argument: Partitioning the joint distribution gives p=θ−e++e−. Nonnegativity and the assumed budgets imply max(0,θ−δ+)≤p≤min(1,θ+δ−). Both endpoints are achievable for every θ∈[0,1]. For the lower endpoint, set e−=0 and e+=min(δ+,θ), assigning the remaining reference-positive mass to true success and all reference-negative mass to failure. For the upper endpoint, set e+=0 and e−=min(δ−,1−θ), assigning all reference-positive mass to success. These assignments have nonnegative cell probabilities summing to one and obey both budgets. Thus no narrower population interval follows from θ and these budgets alone, including at θ=0 or θ=1.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct a task-cluster audit without run-level independence
reasoning_steps.argument: Sample n independent task clusters from D, with independent cluster-level execution randomness and no shared mutable state across clusters. Execute the fixed r-run protocol within each cluster; dependence within a cluster is unrestricted. Independently select J_i uniformly from {1,…,r} for each cluster, without selecting on outcomes, and reference-label that execution. Then T_i=R_i,J_i are independent Bernoulli variables with common mean θ. Every attempted execution remains in the sampling frame. Missing selected labels must be obtained or conservatively represented, not silently dropped. This sampling construction targets a uniformly selected run, not best-of-r success or probability that every run succeeds.

reasoning_steps.title: Add finite-sample uncertainty
reasoning_steps.argument: Let θhat=(1/n)Σ_i T_i, choose 0<α<1 before seeing outcomes, and set t=sqrt(log(2/α)/(2n)). For independent variables in [0,1], the centered-sum moment-generating-function bound E exp(λΣ_i(T_i−θ))≤exp(nλ²/8), followed by Markov's inequality and minimization over λ, gives each tail probability at most exp(−2nt²). A union bound therefore gives |θhat−θ|≤t with probability at least 1−α. On that event, Step 2 yields p∈[max(0,θhat−t−δ+), min(1,θhat+t+δ−)]. Coverage is conditional on the validity of the error budgets and sampling assumptions; it does not certify them. If independently estimated error-budget bounds hold jointly with probability at least 1−β, a union bound gives coverage at least 1−α−β, even if the two estimation procedures are dependent.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive an exact all-pass certification rule
reasoning_steps.argument: For a fixed n and one-sided confidence level 1−α, define a lower bound for θ to be α^(1/n) if all n selected reference labels pass, and zero otherwise. If θ<α^(1/n), the only event on which this bound exceeds θ is all-pass, whose probability is θ^n<α; otherwise it never exceeds θ. Subtracting δ+ and clipping at zero gives a valid lower bound for p. To make this all-pass bound reach p≥1−ε, where 0≤δ+<ε<1, it suffices to choose n≥ceil(log(α)/log(1−ε+δ+)). When δ+≥ε, this rule cannot reach the target at any finite n. The calculation exposes a reference-error floor: more reference-labeled runs cannot by themselves remove uncertainty about false certification.

reasoning_steps.title: Show why neither repetition nor judge agreement supplies the missing premises
reasoning_steps.argument: For task heterogeneity, let independent task types B_i be Bernoulli(1/2), and let all r labels within task i equal B_i. The mean of all nr labels is then (1/n)Σ_i B_i and has variance 1/(4n), not the independent-run variance 1/(4nr). In one world Y=1 always; in the other Y=0 always. All observed R,Z data, including repeated agreement, are identical, while p is respectively one and zero. Therefore agreement alone cannot establish a nontrivial δ+ or identify actual reliability.

reasoning_steps.argument: The result replaces perfect-reference correctness with explicit error allowances and supplies a reproducible audit unit, confidence interval, and all-pass sample-size rule. reasoning_steps.argument: Define S=(B,D,Q,W,A,V). B is a durable sequence of actual business effects, each with a unique receipt, operation key k, and full canonical payload p. reasoning_steps.title: Define network and crash transitions
reasoning_steps.argument: SEND appends an envelope (delivery ID,k,p) to Q without changing B or D. DROP permanently removes an undelivered envelope; a dropped request can never commit later. HOLD leaves an envelope pending, permitting later delivery: a timeout is not cancellation. DELIVER removes an envelope from Q and starts service work W. Responses may independently be delivered, dropped, or held. TIMEOUT adds a fixed tool-visible timeout at a prescribed logical time, without asserting any server state. A service crash clears W but preserves durable B and D; queued envelopes remain unless an explicit network fault removes them. An agent crash restores its declared checkpoint and clears volatile memory, without undoing B, D, or pending requests. These rules make delayed work distinct from work known to have been discarded.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the three service variants
reasoning_steps.argument: ORDINARY appends a fresh effect to B on each successful request and then emits its receipt. ATOMIC serializes requests: if D lacks k, one durable transition appends an effect e=(receipt,k,p) to B and sets D[k]=(p,receipt); if D contains the same payload, it emits the stored receipt without another effect; a different payload yields a conflict without mutation. A crash during the atomic transition has only a before or after outcome. For explicit negative controls, EFFECT_FIRST checks D, durably appends the effect, then separately writes D; RECORD_FIRST checks D, durably writes D using a reserved receipt, then separately appends the effect. In both naive split variants a matching D entry unconditionally suppresses execution and returns its receipt. RECORD_FIRST therefore deliberately has no pending-state reconciliation. These definitions do not cover all possible nontransactional protocols.

SEND, network transitions, timeouts, and agent crashes leave B and D unchanged. An atomic new-key commit adds exactly the corresponding pair; a matching replay and a conflict change neither object. output.claim: For a single operation with stable identity and payload, atomic durable coupling of its external effect and deduplication record guarantees at most one effect despite duplicate delivery and crashes; it guarantees exactly one effect only if some request eventually commits. In contrast, two naive implementations that write the effect and terminal success record separately admit explicit crash traces producing either two effects or zero effects. output.method: Specify a small transition system and manually derive discriminating traces. Hypothesis: local checkpoint restoration alone does not repair ambiguous external commitment, while an atomic effect-and-record transition prevents duplicates within its stated scope. Compare ordinary retry, effect-first recording, record-first recording, and atomic deduplication using the same operation, payload, fault schedule, agent policy, and resource caps. The discriminating outcome is an independently audited external-effect count, not a completion message or deduplication-table entry. Include no-fault, lost-request, lost-acknowledgment, delayed-request, crash, concurrency, and payload-mismatch controls. Both runtimes are unavailable; no implementation or experiment was executed. reasoning_steps.title: 1. Scope and treatment of the prior finding
reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied extract of artifact 984e8fd3-f76b-46fb-b868-378c2f103425 concerns one non-idempotent external operation and ambiguous commitment. That domain matches this proposed mechanism test, but not arbitrary multi-step agent tasks. Adopt its proposed separation of local observations from external effects as a modeling requirement, not an observed property. Its original artifact, some assumptions, and additional notes are unavailable; one other prior finding is omitted. Consequently, the following transition rules and conclusions are stated and derived independently rather than importing the extract's sufficient-repair assertion. The saved request for an auditable trace suite is addressed at specification level only.

reasoning_steps.title: 2. Define separate durable, visible, and audit state
reasoning_steps.argument: For one intended operation, let k be its identity and p its immutable payload. State is (E,D,Q,C,V,J). E is the actual durable business-effect ledger; N(k,p) counts its effects. D is a durable map from identity to a terminal record (payload,result). Q holds undelivered request and response messages, with distinct transport delivery IDs even when k is shared. C is the agent's durable checkpoint, initially containing (k,p,intent); V is its full accessible transcript, including tool fields and accessible timing. J is evaluator-only instrumentation recording delivery, commit, crash, and effect events. Neither E, D, Q, nor J is available to the agent in this experiment except through specified tool responses. The evaluator reads E independently of D. Actual task correctness is one matching effect and no conflicting effect for the intended operation; an agent's claimed completion and receipt of a valid acknowledgment are separate measured variables.

reasoning_steps.title: 3. Define transport and service transitions
reasoning_steps.argument: Send enqueues request (k,p). Drop permanently removes that message before service acceptance; delay leaves it eligible for later delivery, even after an agent timeout or restart. A timeout appends the specified timeout event to V and does not cancel Q. An ordinary service delivery appends one effect to E and then may enqueue an acknowledgment. In the atomic service, handling an absent k commits one indivisible durable update that appends its effect and installs D[k]=(p,r); an existing matching entry returns r without an effect; an existing entry with a different payload returns a conflict without an effect. Operations on the same k are serialized. A service crash preserves committed durable state, loses uncommitted work, and cannot split the atomic transition. Agent restoration changes C and volatile agent state, not E or D, and does not cancel outstanding transport messages. No compensation, authoritative agent lookup, or external writer is included.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Derive the atomic invariant and distinguish safety from liveness
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially E and D are empty. For requests sharing the same k and p, the invariant is N(k,p)=1 exactly when D[k] exists, and otherwise N(k,p)=0. An absent-key atomic commit changes both sides from zero to one; matching duplicate delivery changes neither; dropping, delaying, response loss, and crashes change neither durable component. Serialization makes one of two concurrent absent-key requests commit first, after which the other sees the record. Induction over these transitions proves N(k,p)≤1 for every finite prefix. If at least one request reaches and completes the absent-key transition, N(k,p)=1 thereafter. Without that delivery/commit condition, all requests may be dropped and N remains zero. Even with N=1, all responses can be lost, so verified completion by the agent additionally requires appropriate response delivery or another trusted confirmation mechanism.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Derive the ambiguous-commit controls
reasoning_steps.argument: Write durable states as (N,d), where d=0 means no record and d=1 means a matching terminal record. Trace T0, no-fault control: ordinary delivery gives (0,0)→(1,0), whereas atomic delivery gives (0,0)→(1,1); each returns an acknowledgment. T1, pre-commit loss: drop the initial request, expose a timeout, then deliver one retry. Ordinary and atomic modes finish with N=1. T2, post-commit acknowledgment loss: commit the initial request, drop its response, expose the same timeout, then deliver one retry. Ordinary mode follows (0,0)→(1,0)→(2,0); atomic mode follows (0,0)→(1,1)→(1,1). Before recovery, T1 and T2 can have identical C and V by construction, although their E differs. With no retry, T1 instead ends at N=0 and T2 at N=1. Thus the controls distinguish recovery choices from external commit history. In an implementation, equality of the complete accessible prefixes must be audited rather than assumed from equal timeout strings.

reasoning_steps.title: 6. Exhibit both split-write crash counterexamples
reasoning_steps.argument: Define the naive effect-first service to check D, append the effect when D is absent, and then write a terminal success record. Trace T3: append effect, crash before the record, recover, and deliver a retry. Durable states are (0,0)→(1,0)→crash→(2,0)→(2,1). The task has a duplicate. Define the naive record-first service to install a terminal success record before executing the effect, and to treat that record as completed on retry. Trace T4: write the record, crash before the effect, recover, and deliver a retry. States are (0,0)→(0,1)→crash→(0,1), with a returned success but no effect. Both follow from the specified rules. These are counterexamples to those two naive implementations, not an impossibility theorem for every multi-write protocol: a pending record, transaction coordinator, reconciliation, or service-native idempotency changes the protocol and requires separate analysis.

reasoning_steps.title: 7. Check delayed requests and the atomic crash boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: Trace T5 delays the initial request rather than dropping it, allows the retry to commit first, then releases the initial request. Ordinary mode produces two effects; atomic mode produces one, regardless of which delivery arrives first. The evaluator must therefore distinguish deadline state from state after scheduled outstanding requests have drained; a temporarily correct N=1 can conceal a later duplicate. Trace T6 crashes the atomic service immediately before or immediately after its commit transition, suppressing any response. The only permitted durable outcomes are (0,0) and (1,1). A reliable subsequent retry takes either to (1,1). Observing (1,0) or (0,1) after recovery would falsify the claimed atomic contract for this modeled operation. This boundary test must inspect the business effect, not merely the service's own success record.

reasoning_steps.title: 8. State scope-changing negative controls
reasoning_steps.argument: Trace T7 submits two concurrent requests with identical k,p: atomic serialization permits one effect, while a non-atomic check-then-act implementation can allow both workers to observe absence and execute twice. Trace T8 retries k with payload p'≠p after the initial commit: the specified service must reject the mismatch and preserve E and D. Trace T9 retries the same intended operation under a new key k', or deletes D[k] before a delayed duplicate arrives: the otherwise atomic service can now create a second effect. T9 does not contradict the invariant, because stable identity or record retention has been removed. Likewise, two distinct legitimate operations must receive distinct keys; key reuse can suppress required work. These controls isolate the system contract from the separate empirical question of whether an agent preserves operation identity through restoration and replanning.

reasoning_steps.title: 9. Specify the discriminating experiment and its evidential limits
reasoning_steps.argument: First run scripted retry policies against T0–T9 to test the harness independently of model behavior. Record the entire exposed prefix, durable E and D after every crash, delivery order, pending requests, effect count at the deadline and after controlled draining, response truthfulness, and all costs. Use evaluator-side operation identity to detect duplicates even if the agent changes keys. Only after these conformance checks should fixed-version agents be tested with paired environments, balanced fault schedules, matched prompts and budgets, and repeated trials. Change the service mechanism alone before adding checkpoint or planning interventions; separately test the agent's identity-preservation rate. Report per-fault verified success, silent false completion, missing and duplicate effects, unfinished work, latency, and tool/monetary cost, including recovery overhead. Paired trial uncertainty and held-out tasks are necessary for an empirical effect estimate; this finite manual suite provides neither a deployment success rate nor coverage of all concurrent or distributed histories.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the operation, objective, and observation boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider an agent instructed to cause exactly one irreversible external effect, such as appending one shipment order. Each accepted ordinary request creates one effect; there is no built-in deduplication. Let N be the external effect count for this task. Correctness is N=1, not merely receiving a plausible response. The agent records the same local intent before sending the request. At a timeout, its accessible checkpoint, messages, and observations do not reveal whether that request committed. Assume the only terminal recovery choices are skip or one retry; the retry, if chosen, commits exactly one additional effect. This intentionally restricted model isolates ambiguous-commit recovery rather than arbitrary tool or model errors.

review.rationale: The operation, success predicate N=1, observation boundary, and restricted terminal actions define a coherent model. They are accepted as premises only because the claim is explicitly conditional on them.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct two indistinguishable fault histories
reasoning_steps.argument: In history H0, the initial request is lost before commitment, leaving N=0. In history H1, the request commits, leaving N=1, but its acknowledgment is lost. Both histories end at the same timeout with the same local intent record and no acknowledgment. By assumption, no authoritative status lookup or other distinguishing observation is available before the decision. Therefore a policy using only that local information must use the same retry probability q in both histories. Random internal reasoning or replanning cannot distinguish two histories when its inputs and randomization distribution are identical.

review.rationale: Given identical accessible histories and identical policy-randomization distributions, a local-information policy must assign the same probability to retrying. H0 and H1 differ only in evaluator-visible external effect count.

reasoning_steps.title: Derive the sharp worst-case error bound
reasoning_steps.argument: In H0, skipping leaves N=0 and retrying yields N=1, so the error probability is e0=1-q. In H1, skipping preserves N=1 and retrying yields N=2, so e1=q. Consequently e0+e1=1 and max(e0,e1)>=1/2. Equality is attained by q=1/2, making the bound sharp within this model. The deterministic edge cases q=0 and q=1 each fail with probability one in one history. This is a worst-case bound over two possible histories, not an assertion that either history occurs equally often in deployment.

review.rationale: Under the stipulated successful retry, H0 fails exactly when the policy skips, whereas H1 fails exactly when it retries. Thus e0=1-q, e1=q, their sum is one, and their maximum is at least one half; q=1/2 attains equality.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate worst-case reliability from deployment-average reliability
reasoning_steps.argument: If H1 has known conditional probability p among ambiguous timeouts, expected error is (1-p)(1-q)+pq. This affine function is minimized at q=1 when p<1/2, at q=0 when p>1/2, and by any q when p=1/2. The minimum is min(p,1-p). Thus an excellent average result can coexist with certain failure in the rarer history. The expression applies only within the ambiguous-timeout population and with equal weighting of missing and duplicate effects; it is not an overall task failure rate or an appropriate loss function when duplicate effects are more harmful.

review.rationale: Weighting the two conditional errors by 1-p and p gives 1-p+(2p-1)q. Its slope yields the stated optimal endpoint policies and minimum min(p,1-p). The equal-loss and ambiguous-timeout conditioning restrictions are explicitly preserved.
